scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Bird-Warrior Dance of Sarawak
This is Ngajat. 16th century to present.
on_screen: Title card: Ngajat · Malaysia · 16th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is believed to have originated in the 16th century.
Ancestors of the Iban community created the movements after observing the footprints of a common hill myna and the wing-spreading behavior of the great argus.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Ngajat is performed during Gawai festivals, to welcome special guests, and historically to celebrate the success of headhunting.
It serves as a display of masculinity, warrior strength, and cultural identity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features graceful, bird-like movements.
Male dancers may use props like swords and shields.
In Ngajat Lesong, a dancer lifts a wooden rice mortar weighing 7 to 20 kilograms with his teeth.
Watch for Bungai Ajat.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dancers stand in a circle or lead a procession.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Musical instruments include large and medium gongs (tawak and bebendai), drums (ketebung/dumba), a set of small gongs (engkromong), and the belikan string instrument.
Listen for the tawak, bebendai, ketebung, dumba.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Male dancers wear 'gagung' (traditionally animal skin, now often goatskin) and feathered headdresses.
Female dancers wear headdresses, chest hooks, waist cloths, and bracelets.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dion Das Louis, an eight-year-old dancer from Sarawak, won two gold medals at the 2024 World Performing Arts Championships.

Variants include Ngajat Serakup (standardized stage version), Ngajat Bebunoh (combat/hunting), Ngajat Lesong (strength), Ngajat Induk (female performance), Ngajat Muka Kuta (mixed gender), and Ngajat Ngalu Temuai (welcoming).
The dance is a traditional Iban practice, with modern stage versions like Ngajat Serakup developed by the Dayak Dance And Cultural Association.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance is part of the Iban tangible and intangible cultural heritage, including ritual processes that are protected by the Malaysian federal and Sarawak state governments.
